title: Notification System (Push / SMS / Email)
problem: Design a system that delivers notifications across push (APNs/FCM), SMS, and email channels at scale, with reliable retries, rate limiting, per-user preferences, and minute-scale latency for transactional messages.
summary: A producer-facing HTTP API accepts notification requests, validates, rate-limits, and writes them to a per-channel queue. Per-channel worker fleets consume and call the appropriate third-party service (APNs for iOS, FCM for Android, SMS vendors like Twilio/Nexmo, email providers like SendGrid/SES). Device tokens, templates, and user settings live in a DB with a cache tier in front. Every attempt is logged to a notifications log/analytics store. The dominant design choice is an async queue between notification servers and workers — this decouples ingest spikes (bulk broadcasts) from the rate-limited, slow, and failure-prone third-party services. Key reliability patterns from the book: (1) dedupe via an idempotency key at the server so repeats aren't double-sent, (2) retry with a retry queue for transient failures, (3) notification log for analytics + audit, (4) rate limiting so users aren't spammed. Sized for 10B notifications/day (~115K/sec sustained, 1M/sec peak for broadcasts).

functional: Accept notification requests via POST /v1/notify with channel hint and template
Deliver across push (APNs/FCM), SMS, and email channels
Support per-user preferences and opt-outs per channel
Dedupe retries via client-supplied idempotency key
Retry transient failures with exponential backoff
Emit per-attempt log rows for analytics and audit
nonFunctional: Sustain 115K notifications/sec average, 1M/sec peak for broadcasts
P99 end-to-end latency under 30 s for transactional push
At-least-once delivery with exactly-once semantics per (user, idempotency_key) for 24 h
99.95% availability of the ingest API independent of vendor outages

assumptions: 10B notifications/day total across all channels (≈ 115K/sec average)
Broadcast campaigns up to 100M recipients in <10 minutes → peak 200K fanout/sec
Per-user rate limit: 10 notifications per minute per user per channel (abuse guard)
Retry policy: exponential backoff at 1m, 5m, 30m, 2h, 12h; drop after 5 attempts
estimates: Push workers: 115K * 0.7 = 80K/sec → at 100ms p50 per APNs/FCM call with connection pooling, ~8K concurrent → 16 workers * 500 each
SMS workers: 115K * 0.1 = 11.5K/sec → Twilio account throughput tier typically 100-600 msg/sec; need to shard across many sub-accounts
Email workers: 115K * 0.2 = 23K/sec → SMTP via SendGrid, pool of ~2K connections
Kafka topics: one per channel, 200 partitions each, 7-day retention → ~3 TB peak storage
Notification log DB (Cassandra): 10B rows/day * 300B ≈ 3 TB/day → 1 PB over a year

producer.name: Services / Clients (producers)
producer.summary: Any internal service or campaign UI that submits notification requests. The book shows 'Service 1..Service N' as producers — any upstream can fire a notification.

sections.heading: Who sends
sections.body:
The book distinguishes three major classes:
1. Transactional — order-confirmed, password-reset, 2FA code (tight latency SLO).
2. Triggered — low-balance, new-follower, friend-request (best-effort).
3. Campaign — marketing blasts, app-update announcements (bulk, minute-scale).
All call the same API with a channel hint.

sections.heading: Request shape
sections.body:
```
POST /v1/notify
{ user_id: 4782, channel: "push"|"sms"|"email"|"auto", template_id: "order_shipped_v3", variables: { order_id: 9921, eta: "Friday" }, idempotency_key: "ord-9921-shipped"
}
```

sections.heading: Why idempotency keys matter
sections.body: Producers retry on 5xx. Without an idempotency key, a successful-but-timed-out POST followed by a retry would deliver the same SMS twice — expensive and annoying. The API dedupes on (user_id, idempotency_key) for 24h. This is the book's 'dedupe' reliability step.

bottlenecks.title: Retry storms on 5xx from Notification API
bottlenecks.trigger: During a Notification API brownout or Kafka unavailability returning 503, all upstream producers (transactional + triggered + campaign) retry simultaneously. At steady-state 115K/sec with naive fixed retries, effective load can 3-5x to 350K-500K/sec, well above the 1M/sec peak budget reserved for legitimate broadcasts.
bottlenecks.symptom: On-call sees Notification API p99 latency spike to seconds, 503 rate climbs, and Kafka producer queue saturates. Duplicate idempotency keys flood the dedupe store; producers log 'retry exhausted' for transactional flows (password reset, 2FA) causing user-visible failures in auth paths.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Mandate exponential backoff with jitter in the producer SDK (base 100ms, cap 10s, decorrelated jitter), cap client-side retries at 3, and honor Retry-After headers from 429/503. Add a client-side circuit breaker (e.g., resilience4j with 50% failure threshold over 20 requests) that sheds non-transactional traffic first.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `notify_client_retry_rate / notify_client_request_rate > 0.1` per producer service for 2 min; track `notify_client_inflight_requests` histogram for queue buildup; dashboard dedupe-hit rate — a sudden climb above 5% indicates producers are retrying successful requests.

bottlenecks.title: Missing or colliding idempotency keys
bottlenecks.trigger: Producers that omit the Idempotency-Key header, generate it from non-unique inputs (e.g., `user_id + timestamp_seconds`), or reuse it across semantically different events. At 115K/sec, even a 0.1% collision rate = 115 wrong-dedupes/sec = ~10M/day silently dropped notifications.
bottlenecks.symptom: User support tickets: 'I never got my order confirmation' while logs show status=noop (deduped). Campaign tools report lower-than-expected delivery counts. SMS spend bill shows double-sends during incident postmortems where producers retried without keys.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce Idempotency-Key as a required header at the API gateway (reject with 400 if missing). Provide a canonical SDK that derives the key as `sha256(tenant_id + domain_event_id + template_id)` — never time-based. Add a lint rule in CI for services calling /v1/notify. Expand dedupe store TTL from 24h to 72h to cover long retry windows.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric `notify_api_missing_idempotency_key_total` with alert >0 (should be zero in prod); dashboard of dedupe-hit rate per producer service — anomaly detection on sudden drops (missing keys) or spikes (retry storm or key collision).

bottlenecks.title: Inline fanout attempts for large segments
bottlenecks.trigger: A producer (e.g., marketing tool, batch job) iterates a 100M-user segment client-side and POSTs 100M individual /v1/notify calls instead of using /v1/notify/broadcast. At even 10K/sec per producer pod, this ties up producer workers for ~2.8 hours and hammers the API's rate limiter.
bottlenecks.symptom: Producer service's own thread pool exhausts, unrelated business logic stalls (e.g., the commerce service can't send order confirmations because its worker pool is busy fanning out a promo). Notification API sees sustained 1M/sec from a single tenant; global rate limiter starts 429ing legitimate transactional traffic.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Route any request with recipient count >10K to /v1/notify/broadcast and reject bulk fanout on /v1/notify with HTTP 413 + guidance. Publish clear SDK helpers `notifyBroadcast(segment_id, template_id)` and deprecate loop-based patterns in code review. Enforce per-tenant concurrency limits (e.g., max 1000 in-flight /v1/notify per tenant) at the API.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `notify_api_requests_per_tenant_per_min > 600_000` (10K/sec sustained) on the single-send endpoint; per-tenant dashboard showing single-send vs broadcast request ratio — flag tenants with >100K single-sends per hour for the same template_id.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why producers are called out as a component In the notification system, the "producer" isn't one service — it's *every* internal system that wants to send a notification: the commerce service firing an order-shipped push, the auth service sending a 2FA SMS, the marketing console launching a 100M-user campaign. The design calls them out as a component because the **contract they follow** (idempotency keys, retry behavior, which endpoint they hit) directly determines whether the rest of the system stays healthy. A notification API is only as reliable as the clients calling it. ## What goes wrong without a disciplined producer contract Imagine the commerce service POSTs "order shipped" to the Notification API, the call times out at 30s, and the service retries 3 times. Without an idempotency key, the user gets the same SMS four times — that's a real $0.04 of wasted spend per user and an angry support ticket. Worse, during a Notification API brownout, *every* producer retrying simultaneously turns 115K/sec of legitimate traffic into 400K/sec of retry storm, which cascades into Kafka backpressure and eventually 2FA codes not arriving during login. ## The scale math The system is sized for **115K notifications/sec average, 1M/sec peak during broadcasts**. If even 0.1% of producer requests have missing or colliding idempotency keys, that's 115 wrong-dedupes/sec × 86,400s ≈ **10M silently-dropped notifications per day**. At this scale, the producer's behavior isn't a minor client concern — it's a first-class reliability surface. ## The trade-off Treating producers as part of the design means enforcing an SDK and header contract across dozens of upstream teams, which is organizational overhead — but it's the only way to keep the async pipeline from drowning in duplicates or retry storms.

api.name: Notification Servers
api.summary: Stateless HTTP service (the book calls these 'notification servers') that validates, resolves user preferences/device tokens/templates, rate-limits, dedupes, and forwards to the per-channel queue.

sections.heading: Responsibilities
sections.body:
- Provide APIs for producing notifications (internal services or admin tooling).
- Basic validation: user_id exists, template exists, variables bound, device token valid.
- Fetch data needed to render — device tokens, notification templates, user settings — from the DB/cache.
- Place a message in the per-channel message queue for parallel processing.
- Return 202 Accepted with a notification_id immediately.

sections.heading: Why 202 not 200
sections.body: Delivery is asynchronous. 202 communicates 'queued, not delivered'. Callers get the notification_id to query status later via GET /v1/notify/:id.

sections.heading: Horizontal scaling
sections.body: Stateless; scale on CPU. Peak 1M/sec during campaigns → with 10ms p50 handling ≈ 10K concurrent → 20 replicas of 500 concurrency each at 40% utilization.

sections.heading: Reliability: dedupe
sections.body: The book explicitly calls out exactly-once-ish semantics via a dedupe step: on receiving a notification event, check if it's a duplicate (by idempotency key or event hash) and drop it if so. Avoids double-sends on producer retries.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Queue unavailable → return 503; producers retry with idempotency key.
- User settings/device cache slow → fall back to DB with local LRU (5s TTL) to absorb hiccups.

bottlenecks.title: Dedupe store hot-path latency at 1M/sec peak
bottlenecks.trigger: During broadcast peaks the API must check the idempotency-key dedupe store on every request. At 1M/sec peak (vs 115K/sec average), a single Redis dedupe cluster doing SET NX PX across a 72h TTL key space sees 1M writes/sec plus TTL bookkeeping. A single Redis shard caps ~100K ops/sec, so anything under 10 shards saturates; cross-AZ RTT of 1-2ms per check adds directly to the API's 5-15ms service budget.
bottlenecks.symptom: API p99 climbs from ~15ms to 100ms+, concurrency (budgeted 5000) backs up, 503s returned to producers, which then retry and amplify load. Dedupe hit-rate metric spikes as retries arrive. Transactional flows (2FA, password reset) miss their minute-scale SLO.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shard the dedupe Redis cluster by hash(idempotency_key) across at least 16 shards sized for 2x peak (2M ops/sec headroom). Use SET NX PX (single round trip, no GET+SET). Co-locate the dedupe cluster in the same AZ as API replicas to keep RTT <0.5ms. For extreme bursts, add an in-process bloom filter per API replica as a negative-cache fast path before hitting Redis.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `notify_api_dedupe_latency_p99 > 5ms` for 1min; `redis_dedupe_ops_per_shard > 80_000/sec` (80% of shard ceiling); `notify_api_p99 > 50ms` with correlation to dedupe step span in tracing.

bottlenecks.title: Cache miss storms on template/device/settings lookups
bottlenecks.trigger: Every request does 3 cache lookups (tpl, dev, set). On a Redis failover, cold deploy, or template edit invalidation, a 1% miss rate at 1M/sec = 10K/sec falling through to the Cassandra DB (budgeted 3K concurrency, 3-12ms service time). A template edit to a popular template (used in a broadcast) causes a stampede — all 200 API replicas miss simultaneously on `tpl:spring_promo_v1`.
bottlenecks.symptom: API latency bimodal — hits stay at 5ms, misses stretch to 50-200ms as DB saturates. Cassandra pending-read queue grows; API concurrency limit (5000) is reached and new requests are rejected with 503. Cascading producer retries multiply the stampede.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use single-flight/request-coalescing per API replica (e.g., Go singleflight, Caffeine refreshAfterWrite) so N concurrent misses for the same key fire one DB read. Add a 5s local LRU in front of Redis to absorb Redis hiccups. On template publish, pre-warm the cache via a fanout to all API replicas before the template becomes active. Use probabilistic early refresh (XFetch) to avoid simultaneous TTL expiry.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric `notify_api_cache_miss_rate` with alert >2% for 30s; `notify_api_db_fallback_qps > 5000`; trace span distribution — if p99/p50 ratio of cache step exceeds 10x, stampede is active.

bottlenecks.title: Head-of-line blocking from slow Kafka produce acks
bottlenecks.trigger: API produces to per-channel Kafka topics with acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2. Under partition leader failover or a slow ISR follower, produce latency jumps from 2-8ms to 500ms+. At 1M/sec peak with 5000 concurrency budget, any produce stall above 5ms violates Little's Law (5000 / 1M = 5ms max service time) and the API starts rejecting requests.
bottlenecks.symptom: API returns 503 even though CPU is idle — threads/goroutines are parked waiting on Kafka acks. Producer SDK metrics show record-send-rate dropping while buffer-available-bytes plummets. Kafka under-replicated-partitions metric correlates with the API brownout.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Keep Kafka producer buffer sized generously (buffer.memory=256MB, linger.ms=5, batch.size=64KB) and set delivery.timeout.ms aggressively (2s) so stuck sends fail fast and shed rather than pile up. Run 3 brokers per topic-partition with rack-aware placement so one AZ loss doesn't drop below min.insync.replicas. Use async produce + bounded outstanding-request queue with load shedding when queue > 80% (return 503 with Retry-After to push backpressure to producers).
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `kafka_producer_record_send_latency_p99 > 50ms` for 1min; `kafka_under_replicated_partitions > 0`; `notify_api_kafka_produce_queue_depth > 10000` per replica; correlate with `notify_api_503_rate`.

prebuild.explanation: ### Why the Notification Servers sit in front of everything For a notification system that ingests from dozens of upstream services (commerce, auth, marketing) and fans out to three very different downstream channels (APNs, FCM, Twilio, SendGrid), you need *one* place that speaks a single clean HTTP contract to producers and hides all the messiness behind it. That's the job of the Notification Servers. They validate the request, resolve the user's device tokens and preferences, check the rate limiter, dedupe on the idempotency key, and drop the event onto the right Kafka topic — then return `202 Accepted` in ~10ms. Without this layer, every producer service would need to know how to talk to APNs, respect quiet hours, and handle Twilio's per-number throughput limits. That's unmaintainable. ### What breaks without it If producers wrote directly to Kafka, a buggy commerce service could flood `notif.sms` with malformed records, bypass the 10-per-minute-per-user rate limit, and send a user the same password-reset SMS four times because it retried on timeout. The operator would see a spike in SMS spend and angry support tickets; the SMS workers would dutifully deliver every duplicate because there's no upstream dedupe. ### The scale math The system is sized for **115K notifications/sec average and 1M/sec peak during broadcasts**. At 10ms p50 per request, Little's Law says you need ~10K concurrent request slots at peak (1M × 0.01s). The design provisions 20 stateless replicas at 500 concurrency each = 10K slots at 40% utilization — headroom for spikes without autoscaling lag. ### The trade-off Adding this hop costs ~10ms of latency and one more tier to operate, but it's the only place where dedupe, preferences, and rate limiting can be enforced uniformly across every producer.

cache.name: Cache (tokens / templates / settings)
cache.summary: Read-through Redis cache for the three hot lookups notification servers do on every request: user device tokens, notification templates, and user notification settings.

sections.heading: Why a cache tier
sections.body: The book explicitly includes 'Cache' in the final diagram. The notification server reads (user → device tokens), (template_id → template body), and (user → settings) on every request. Caching collapses 3 DB reads to 3 sub-ms Redis gets for the hot set.

sections.heading: Data structures
Invalidation
sections.body:
- Device token changes (re-register, uninstall) → publish invalidation to Redis on write.
- Template edits are rare — longer TTL (5 min) is fine.

bottlenecks.title: Hot-key stampede on popular template invalidation
bottlenecks.trigger: A marketing team publishes a new version of a broadcast template (e.g., `tpl:spring_promo_v1`) mid-campaign, invalidating the key right when 200 API replicas are reading it at broadcast peak (1M req/sec). All 200 replicas miss simultaneously on the same key and stampede the single Cassandra row holding that template.
bottlenecks.symptom: Cache MGET latency stays ~1ms on `dev:*` and `set:*` but the `tpl:*` part of the MGET spikes to 50-200ms p99. Cassandra shows a single-partition hot read at 10K+ qps. API p99 degrades from 15ms to 100ms+ for 5-30s until the key is repopulated; producers see 503s as the API concurrency budget (5000) is consumed by stalled requests.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use probabilistic early refresh (XFetch) on template keys so replicas refresh ~10s before TTL independently; combine with per-replica single-flight (Go singleflight / Caffeine) to coalesce concurrent misses to one DB read per replica. On template publish, explicitly pre-warm all replicas via a fanout invalidate+load RPC before the new version is referenced in any notification.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `redis_cache_miss_rate{key_prefix="tpl"} > 1%` for 30s; per-key hot-key detector (`redis-cli --hotkeys` or Redis 6 client-side key stats); Cassandra `ReadLatency` on `notif_templates` table p99 > 20ms.

bottlenecks.title: Redis shard saturation at 1M req/sec × 3 lookups
bottlenecks.trigger: At broadcast peak of 1M API req/sec, each request issues an MGET over 3 keys (tpl, dev, set) — that's 3M logical key lookups/sec. A single Redis node tops out around 100K ops/sec; without sharding, a 6-node cluster is already at ceiling with zero headroom for retries or fanout worker lookups.
bottlenecks.symptom: Redis `instantaneous_ops_per_sec` pegs near the shard limit, CPU on Redis nodes saturates at ~100%, and GET latency climbs from 1ms p50 to 5-10ms. The sim's `concurrency: 10000` slot pool fills, causing API read stalls and downstream 503s. Under partial saturation, tail latency reaches 20-50ms, blowing the API's 5-15ms service budget.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shard across at least 20 Redis nodes with consistent hashing (client-side or Redis Cluster), keyed by user_id for `dev:*`/`set:*` and by template_id for `tpl:*`. Size for 2x peak (6M ops/sec → 60 shards worth of headroom). Co-locate Redis with API replicas in the same AZ to keep RTT <0.5ms. Enable client-side caching (Redis 6 RESP3 tracking) for `tpl:*` since templates change rarely.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on per-shard `redis_instantaneous_ops_per_sec > 80_000` for 1min; `redis_used_cpu_sys` > 80%; API tracing span `cache.mget.p99 > 5ms`; uneven shard load (max/min ops ratio > 3x) signals poor key distribution.

bottlenecks.title: Stale device tokens causing silent push failures
bottlenecks.trigger: A user uninstalls the app or the OS rotates the device token. The `dev:{user_id}` cache entry still holds the old token until invalidation propagates or TTL expires. If invalidation pub/sub is dropped (Redis partition, missed message), stale tokens persist for the full TTL; at 115K push/sec, even 0.5% stale rate = ~500/sec pushes sent to dead tokens.
bottlenecks.symptom: Push workers see an elevated rate of APNs `BadDeviceToken` / FCM `UNREGISTERED` 4xx responses. Delivery dashboard shows per-user `sent` status but users report not receiving notifications. On-call traces to cache returning tokens that DB has already marked invalid.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Short TTL on `dev:*` (60s max) with background refresh; on token registration/deregistration, do a synchronous write-through to cache (not just pub/sub invalidation) plus a Redis `DEL` in the same transaction as the DB update. Workers should negative-cache BadDeviceToken responses and publish an invalidation back to the API cache so the stale entry is evicted within one hop.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `apns_bad_device_token_rate / apns_send_rate > 0.5%` for 5min; compare cache-sourced token count vs DB device_count per user in a daily reconciliation job; track `cache_invalidation_pubsub_lag` — drops or pauses indicate propagation failure.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why there's a cache sitting in front of the database For a notification system pushing **115K notifications/sec average and 1M/sec at broadcast peak**, every single request needs the same three pieces of data before it can do anything useful: the user's device tokens (where do I send this?), the template body (what do I say?), and the user's settings (are they even opted in? are they in quiet hours?). Without a cache, every notification triggers three database reads against Cassandra — and Cassandra is sized for durability and capacity, not for answering the same "what's user 4782's device token?" question a thousand times per second. ## What breaks without it If the API talked straight to the database, a marketing broadcast to 100M users would fire 300M DB reads in ~10 minutes. Cassandra would saturate, read latency would climb from 3-12ms into the hundreds of milliseconds, and the API's 5-15ms budget would blow up. Operators would see API p99 spike and 503s flood back to producers; users would see their 2FA codes arrive minutes late — violating the core "minute-scale latency for transactional messages" requirement — because auth traffic is stuck behind a marketing broadcast. ## The arithmetic At 1M req/sec peak × 3 lookups = **3M key lookups/sec**. Redis handles ~100K ops/sec per shard, so ~20 shards at 1-3ms each keeps lookups under a combined ~5ms. The same load hitting Cassandra (3-12ms, 3K concurrency budget) would back up instantly — Little's Law says 3M/sec × 0.008s = 24K concurrent reads needed, 8x over budget. ## The trade-off Caching means accepting brief staleness — a user who just disabled push might get one more notification before the invalidation propagates. For this system, that's an acceptable cost to keep the hot path fast.

db.name: Notification DB (users / devices / settings / templates)
db.summary: Source-of-truth store for user profiles, device tokens, per-user notification settings, and the notification-template catalog. The book explicitly lists these four tables behind the notification servers.

sections.heading: Tables (book's schema)
sections.body:
```
TABLE users (user_id PK, email, phone, locale,...)
TABLE devices (device_id PK, user_id, token, platform -- iOS/Android, last_seen)
TABLE notif_settings (user_id PK, channel, opt_in, quiet_hours_start, quiet_hours_end)
TABLE notif_templates(template_id PK, channel, body, variables_schema, version)
```

sections.heading: Why it's called out separately
sections.body: The notification server needs this data on every request, but it isn't hot enough to live only in cache. Having a durable primary with a cache in front is the standard read-heavy pattern.

sections.heading: Choice
sections.body: Cassandra (or DynamoDB) is the book's implicit choice — PK lookups, huge user fleets, multi-DC. MySQL sharded by `user_id` works if you're already there.

gained: Strong consistency for user settings edits
lost: Resharding is painful at billion-user scale

bottlenecks.title: Cache-miss read amplification during Redis failover or cold start
bottlenecks.trigger: API does 3 lookups per request (tpl, dev, set). At 1M req/sec peak, even a 1% cache miss rate = 30K reads/sec to this DB, exceeding the budgeted 3K concurrency at 3-12ms service time (Little's Law: 30K × 0.008s = 240 concurrent, fine on paper but a 5% miss = 150K/sec = 1200 concurrent, saturating). A Redis shard failover or cold deploy can push miss rate to 20-50% transiently.
bottlenecks.symptom: Cassandra read latency climbs from 3-12ms p99 to 100ms+, pending-read queue grows, API p99 blows past 15ms budget and returns 503s. On-call sees Cassandra `ReadLatency` alerts on `notif_devices` and `notif_templates` tables simultaneously; coordinator nodes show heap pressure from queued reads.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Size Cassandra for 10% miss-rate worst case (30 nodes vs 20). Use LOCAL_QUORUM with speculative retry (`99p`) to hide slow replicas. Add a request-coalescing layer (singleflight) at the API so N concurrent misses for the same key issue one DB read. Pin hot templates in a dedicated small-row-cache keyspace with `rows_per_partition=100` row cache enabled.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `cassandra_ReadLatency{table=~"notif_.*"}_p99 > 25ms` for 1min; `cassandra_pending_reads > 100` per node; correlate with `redis_cache_miss_rate` — if DB QPS spikes while miss rate does, the DB is the bottleneck, not the cache.

bottlenecks.title: Hot partition on popular templates and power-user device rows
bottlenecks.trigger: `notif_templates` is keyed by template_id; a single broadcast template (e.g., `spring_promo_v1`) used in a 100M-user campaign becomes a single-partition hot read. Similarly, a power user with 50+ registered devices has an oversized `devices` partition that gets read on every notification. At broadcast peak with a 1% miss rate on that one template = 10K reads/sec hitting one Cassandra partition (single-partition ceiling ~5K reads/sec).
bottlenecks.symptom: One Cassandra node shows 90%+ CPU while peers are idle — classic hot-partition signature. `nodetool tablehistograms` shows a single partition in the 99th percentile for reads/sec. Template lookups time out for that specific `template_id` while unrelated lookups are fine. Broadcast fanout stalls.
bottlenecks.mitigation: For `notif_templates`, replicate hot templates across N synthetic partition keys (`template_id#0`... `template_id#15`) and have the API pick one at random — spreads reads across 16 partitions. Alternatively, move templates to a tiny dedicated store (DynamoDB on-demand, or just keep them pinned in every API replica's local LRU since they change rarely). For `devices`, cap devices-per-user at 20 and archive older ones.
bottlenecks.detection: `nodetool tablehistograms notif_templates` showing >5K reads/sec on a single partition; alert on per-node CPU skew (`max(cpu) / avg(cpu) > 2`); Cassandra `HotPartitionDetector` if using DataStax, or custom metric on `cassandra_tombstone_scanned_histogram` per partition.

bottlenecks.title: Write amplification from device-token churn
bottlenecks.trigger: Devices re-register tokens on app launch, OS upgrade, and reinstall. At 1B+ MAU with ~10% weekly reinstall/upgrade churn, that's ~14M device-row writes/day, plus cache-invalidation pub/sub traffic on every write. During major iOS/Android releases, churn can 10x to 140M writes/day (~1.6K/sec sustained, 10K/sec bursts) — each write also invalidates the Redis cache entry, causing a read-storm on the next notification to that user.
bottlenecks.symptom: Post-iOS-release traffic: Cassandra compaction pressure on `notif_devices` increases, SSTable count per read climbs, read latency degrades from 3-12ms to 20-40ms. Redis `dev:*` miss rate jumps for affected users; API sees a coincident latency bump. Stale tokens cause elevated APNs `BadDeviceToken` responses at the worker fleet.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use LeveledCompactionStrategy on `notif_devices` (read-heavy table with updates) instead of default STCS to keep read amplification bounded. Batch device updates in a 1s window at the API so rapid reconnects don't write 10x. On write, use cache write-through (not just invalidate) so the next read doesn't miss. Consider separating rarely-changing user profile fields from high-churn device_tokens into two tables to keep compaction scoped.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `cassandra_CompactionPending{table="notif_devices"} > 20`; `cassandra_SSTablesPerReadHistogram_p99 > 5`; device-write rate dashboard with anomaly detection around OS release dates; `apns_bad_device_token_rate > 0.5%` as a downstream indicator of stale cache from missed invalidations.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Notification DB sits behind everything For a notification system fanning messages across push, SMS, and email, every single request needs four pieces of durable truth before it can do anything: *who is this user* (email/phone), *what devices have they registered* (APNs/FCM tokens), *what have they opted into* (push yes, SMS no, quiet hours 11pm–7am), and *what does this template actually say* (the body with variable slots). None of that can live only in cache — device tokens change when users reinstall the app, preferences change when they hit "unsubscribe," and templates are edited by marketing. You need a source of truth that outlives any Redis eviction or crash. ## What happens without it If the system relied only on cache, a Redis failover would mean the Notification API has no idea which devices belong to which users. Users would either stop receiving notifications entirely, or — worse — receive them on *dead* tokens because nothing remembers that a device unregistered. Operators would see APNs `BadDeviceToken` errors spike to 100% while support tickets flood in about missed 2FA codes. The cache layer becomes useless without a backing store to repopulate from. ## The scale math The system is sized for **10B notifications/day ≈ 115K/sec average**, with 3 lookups per request (template, devices, settings) = **345K lookups/sec**. The cache handles the hot path, but even at a modest 1% miss rate that's 3,450 reads/sec hitting this DB — right at the budgeted 3K concurrency at 3–12ms. Cassandra's PK-lookup model handles that comfortably; a relational join-heavy DB would not. ## The trade-off Having a separate durable store adds an extra tier to operate, but it's the only way preferences and device tokens survive a cache wipe.

ratelimit.name: Rate Limiter
ratelimit.summary: Per-user, per-channel token-bucket limiter backed by Redis.

sections.heading: Algorithm
sections.body: Token bucket: 10 tokens/minute/(user,channel), burst capacity 10. Lua script runs atomically in Redis — SCAN + DECRBY + EXPIRE in a single round trip.

sections.heading: Global + per-tenant caps
sections.body: In addition to per-user, a global per-tenant limit protects downstream gateways. Exceeding it causes 429 to the producer with Retry-After.

sections.heading: Why separate from the API
sections.body: Calling it out makes it swappable (Redis → Memcached + CAS, or Envoy's ratelimit service). The API treats it as a cheap yes/no.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body: - Redis partition → fail-open (allow) or fail-closed (deny) depending on criticality; transactional traffic usually fails open with an alert.

lost: Not shared across replicas — effective limit = configured * replicas

bottlenecks.title: Redis Lua script throughput ceiling at 1M req/sec peak
bottlenecks.trigger: Every /v1/notify call runs a token-bucket Lua script (INCR + EXPIRE) against the rate-limit Redis cluster. At broadcast peak of 1M req/sec, a single Redis node caps at ~100K ops/sec for Lua-evaluated commands (single-threaded event loop, Lua blocks all other ops). With under 10 shards the cluster saturates; with 1-2ms cross-AZ RTT added per EVAL, the rate limiter's 1-3ms budget blows out.
bottlenecks.symptom: Rate-limit Redis shows 100% CPU on hot shards, EVAL latency p99 climbs from 1ms to 20-50ms, API p99 degrades past its 15ms budget and returns 503s. Producers retry, amplifying load and worsening the saturation. Transactional flows (2FA, password reset) miss the minute-scale SLO because the limiter is blocking the hot path.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shard the rate-limit Redis cluster by hash(user_id, channel) across at least 16 nodes sized for 2x peak (2M ops/sec headroom). Co-locate shards with API replicas in the same AZ (RTT <0.5ms). Prefer a single atomic command (`SET NX EX` + `INCR` pattern) over multi-op Lua where possible. For extreme bursts, add an in-process approximate token bucket per API replica as a first-level allow filter before hitting Redis.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on per-shard `redis_instantaneous_ops_per_sec > 80_000` for 1min; `redis_used_cpu_sys > 80%`; `ratelimit_eval_latency_p99 > 5ms` for 30s; uneven shard load (max/min ops ratio > 3x) indicates bad key distribution or a hot tenant.

bottlenecks.title: Hot-key contention on per-tenant global limits
bottlenecks.trigger: In addition to per-user buckets, the design enforces per-tenant global caps to protect downstream gateways. A single large tenant (e.g., the commerce service at ~50K/sec, or marketing during a 100M broadcast at 200K/sec) funnels all its limit checks through one key like `rl:tenant:commerce`. That single key lands on one Redis shard, creating a hot-partition bottleneck independent of overall cluster sharding.
bottlenecks.symptom: One Redis node CPU pegs at 100% while peers are idle — classic hot-key signature. All tenant-A traffic stalls at the rate limiter even though the cluster as a whole has capacity. During broadcasts, the marketing tenant's global limit becomes the binding constraint on the entire system and legitimate transactional traffic from other tenants also backs up if they share a Lua script execution slot.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use sliding-window counters split across N sub-keys per tenant (`rl:tenant:commerce:0..15`) with the API randomly picking one shard per request and aggregating allowances probabilistically; accept a small over/under shoot (1-5%) in exchange for 16x spread. Alternatively, implement a hierarchical limiter: coarse in-process counters per API replica that periodically sync a small delta to Redis, avoiding per-request hot-key hits.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-key hot-key detection via `redis-cli --hotkeys` or Redis 6 client-side key stats; alert on per-shard CPU skew (`max(cpu)/avg(cpu) > 2`); dashboard of per-tenant 429 rate — if one tenant dominates 429s while cluster ops/sec is below ceiling, hot-keying is the cause.

bottlenecks.title: Fail-open/fail-closed ambiguity during Redis partition
bottlenecks.trigger: The limiter's documented failure mode is 'fail-open for transactional, fail-closed otherwise' but this requires the API to know the call's criticality on every hop and requires the limiter client to reliably detect Redis unreachability (vs slow). During a Redis AZ partition or failover (30-60s), the API either stalls waiting for timeouts or makes wrong fail decisions at 1M req/sec — allowing 60M unfiltered requests through (abuse risk, SMS-spend blowout) or denying 60M legitimate requests (2FA outages).
bottlenecks.symptom: During a Redis failover: SMS spend spikes because per-user 10/min caps are bypassed (fail-open path) and users report receiving 50+ duplicate SMS; or conversely, 2FA codes stop being delivered and login failure rate jumps (fail-closed path). Post-incident review shows the limiter client used a 1s default timeout, pushing latency into API's budget before the fallback kicked in.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Set an aggressive limiter-client timeout (50ms max) with a short-circuit fallback to a per-replica in-memory approximate bucket sized at `configured_limit / replica_count * 1.2`. Tag each request with criticality (transactional/triggered/campaign) at the API edge so fail-open applies only to transactional. Run the limiter Redis cluster with 3 replicas per shard and rack-aware placement; use Redis Sentinel or Cluster with <5s failover.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `ratelimit_client_timeout_rate > 0.1%` for 30s; `ratelimit_fallback_invoked_total` spike; post-partition reconciliation metric comparing cluster-allowed vs fallback-allowed counts — divergence >10% indicates the fallback path is too permissive or too strict.

prebuild.explanation: ### Why a rate limiter sits in front of this notification system Notifications are uniquely dangerous among API traffic: every request your system accepts costs real money (SMS is ~$0.01/msg) and real user patience (getting the same push 12 times in 5 minutes is how apps get uninstalled). The design commits to "10 notifications per minute per user per channel" as an abuse guard — but that guarantee has to be enforced *somewhere*, and it has to be enforced *before* the message hits Kafka, because once it's queued the workers will dutifully deliver it. The rate limiter is that enforcement point. It also protects downstream: Twilio accounts have hard per-second caps, and if a buggy producer loops and fires 50K SMS/sec at one user, you want to reject it at the edge, not discover it on next month's bill. ### What happens without it A password-reset service has a bug and retries aggressively. User 4782 gets 200 SMS in one minute. The operator sees Twilio spend spike, angry support tickets pour in, and the carrier flags your sending numbers as spam — which now degrades delivery for *every* user on that number pool. The SMS workers, Kafka, and Twilio gateway all did exactly what they were told; the missing guardrail was upstream. ### The scale math At 115K notifications/sec sustained and 1M/sec peak during broadcasts, the limiter runs on every single request. That's why it lives in Redis with a Lua script — a ~1-3ms atomic check. One DB call per request would add 5-15ms to the hot path and blow the API's 10ms budget; a synchronous Twilio quota check would be even worse. ### The trade-off Putting the limiter in its own tier adds a network hop and a shared Redis dependency, but centralizing it (versus an in-process bucket per API replica) is the only way a "10/min per user" limit actually means 10/min when you have 20 API replicas.

queue.name: Per-Channel Queues (+ Retry Queue)
queue.summary: Durable log that decouples notification servers from third-party services. The book diagrams one queue per channel so they scale independently; also an explicit retry queue for transient failures.

sections.heading: Why one queue per channel
sections.body: If iOS, Android, SMS, and email shared a queue, an outage of APNs would back up SMS too. Per-channel queues isolate failure domains and let each worker fleet scale independently against its downstream's characteristics.

sections.heading: Topic layout
sections.body:
- `notif.push` — 200 partitions, key = user_id
- `notif.sms` — 100 partitions, key = user_id
- `notif.email`— 100 partitions, key = user_id
- `notif.retry`— 50 partitions, key = notification_id (for deferred retries)

sections.heading: Retry queue
sections.body: The book explicitly adds a retry queue for failures: on a non-permanent error, the worker publishes the event back to the retry queue with an attempt counter; a scheduled consumer re-delivers after backoff. Drop-and-alert after a fixed number of retries to avoid hammering a broken provider.

sections.heading: Retention & delivery
sections.body: 7-day retention. `acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2`. Consumers commit offsets after the gateway returns a terminal response (success or permanent failure).

sections.heading: Why partitioning by user_id
sections.body: Preserves per-user ordering (you don't want a shipping notification to arrive before the order-confirmation) and lets the worker batch by user for APNs collapse keys.

lost: No ordering except in FIFO queues (limited throughput)
At-least-once semantics + visibility timeouts are trickier than Kafka offsets

gained: Rich routing (topics, headers) out of the box
lost: Throughput ceiling lower than Kafka for this scale

bottlenecks.title: Partition hot-spotting from power users and broadcast keying
bottlenecks.trigger: notif.push uses key=user_id across 200 partitions. During a 100M-user broadcast fanout at ~200K/sec, hash distribution is uniform on average but power users (celebrities, shared accounts) and skewed segment samples concentrate on specific partitions. A single Kafka partition tops out around 10-30MB/s or ~10K msgs/sec; a 2-3x skew pushes hot partitions past 30K msgs/sec while peers sit at 5K.
bottlenecks.symptom: Consumer lag grows on specific partitions (e.g., partition 87 at 2M lag) while others drain normally. Push delivery for users hashed to hot partitions falls behind by 10+ minutes, violating the minute-scale transactional SLO. Kafka broker hosting the hot partition shows disk I/O saturation and elevated produce latency; ISR shrinks as followers can't keep up.
bottlenecks.mitigation: For broadcasts, override keying with key=notification_id (not user_id) to spread load uniformly — per-user ordering isn't meaningful in a broadcast anyway. For transactional traffic keep key=user_id but bump notif.push to 400 partitions to halve per-partition load. Enable Kafka's rack-aware rebalancing and monitor per-partition throughput; add a 'hot-user' detector that rehashes known-skewed user_ids with a salt.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `kafka_consumer_lag{topic="notif.push"}` max/avg ratio > 3x for 2min; per-partition `kafka_server_BrokerTopicMetrics_MessagesInPerSec` stddev anomaly; broker disk write IOPS skew across the cluster.

bottlenecks.title: Retry queue scheduling storm after a multi-hour gateway outage
bottlenecks.trigger: notif.retry has 50 partitions and holds records scheduled with delays up to 12h (attempt 5). During an APNs or Twilio regional brownout lasting 30+ minutes at 80K/sec push rate, ~144M records accumulate in notif.retry with scheduled_at values clustered within the same 1m/5m/30m backoff windows. When the gateway recovers, the retry-scheduler loop tries to republish tens of millions of records to notif.push within seconds, creating a thundering-herd that doubles normal load.
bottlenecks.symptom: Post-outage: notif.push ingestion spikes to 2-3x normal (160-240K/sec), exceeding worker drain capacity; consumer lag balloons to tens of millions; transactional traffic queues behind retried campaign messages. Retry scheduler itself becomes a bottleneck, sequentially scanning partitions and unable to keep up. Second-order failure: gateway, barely recovered, is hammered again and brown-outs a second time.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add decorrelated jitter to backoff delays (e.g., `delay = base * 2^n * random(0.5, 1.5)`) so retries don't align on minute boundaries. Implement a leaky-bucket republisher that caps retry-to-main republish rate at 20% of main topic capacity (16K/sec for push). Use Kafka's per-topic quota feature to throttle notif.retry consumer groups. Prioritize transactional retries over campaign retries via separate retry topics per criticality class.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `kafka_producer_record_send_rate{topic="notif.push",source="retry-scheduler"} > 20000` for 1min; retry queue depth growth rate `rate(notif_retry_lag[5m]) > 100000`; post-recovery monitor on main-topic lag acceleration within 30s of circuit-breaker close events.

bottlenecks.title: Storage blowup on 7-day retention during sustained backlog or broadcast
bottlenecks.trigger: notif.push sized at 200 partitions × 7-day retention is budgeted ~3TB peak. At 115K/sec average with ~500B records × 86400s × 7d = ~35TB/day uncompressed across all channels; the 3TB estimate assumes aggressive compression (5-10x with snappy/zstd) and steady-state drain. During a 100M broadcast + simultaneous APNs brownout, records pile up undelivered and retention-anchored log segments grow 3-5x normal; a sustained 2h worker outage at 80K/sec adds ~300GB of un-acked records.
bottlenecks.symptom: Kafka broker disks cross 80% utilization watermark; log segment rolling slows; under-replicated-partitions metric climbs as followers fall behind on disk-bound IO. In the worst case, disk fills and Kafka stops accepting produces, causing API to return 503 and producers to retry — cascading failure. Compaction/deletion lags, and attempts to raise retention to debug an incident cause further disk pressure.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use tiered storage (Kafka 3.6+ or Confluent Tiered Storage) to offload segments >1h old to S3, keeping only recent hot data on broker SSDs. Enforce topic-level `retention.bytes` quota (e.g., 500GB/partition hard cap) as a safety net alongside time-based retention. Monitor and alarm at 70% disk; auto-expand by pre-provisioning +30% headroom brokers for peak season. For notif.retry specifically, use a shorter retention (48h) since records are republished well before that.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `kafka_log_size_bytes / disk_capacity > 0.7` per broker; `kafka_controller_under_replicated_partitions > 0` for 5min; growth rate `rate(kafka_log_size_bytes{topic="notif.push"}[30m])` exceeding baseline by 2x; daily capacity-forecasting job projecting disk-full date < 3 days.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why there's a queue between the API and the workers For a notification system delivering across push, SMS, and email, the API accepts requests at the speed of the *internet* (producers fire whenever a user places an order, logs in, or a campaign launches) but the workers can only deliver at the speed of *third-party gateways* (APNs, Twilio, SendGrid) — which are slow (50–500ms per call), rate-limited per account, and occasionally brown out for minutes at a time. If the API called these gateways synchronously, every producer would be waiting on Twilio. The queue absorbs this mismatch: API writes land in Kafka in ~5ms and return 202, while workers drain at whatever pace the gateways allow. Having *one queue per channel* means an APNs outage doesn't back up SMS traffic — their failures are isolated. ## What breaks without it Imagine Twilio has a 10-minute brownout. Without a queue, every SMS call from the API hangs for 30s until timing out. Those hung requests hold API connections, the thread pool exhausts, and suddenly *push* and *email* requests also fail because the API itself is unresponsive. Operators would see a global outage; users would miss 2FA codes even though Apple's APNs is perfectly healthy. ## The scale math The design targets **115K notifications/sec average and up to 1M/sec during a 100M-user broadcast**. A broadcast can't fan out inline — the API would melt. Instead, Kafka buffers 100M records in ~8 minutes (200 partitions × ~1K msgs/sec each), and workers drain steadily afterward. Without a buffer, you'd need 10× the worker fleet sized for peak that only happens occasionally. ## Trade-off The queue adds seconds of delivery latency and an extra durable system to operate, but it's the only way to decouple burst ingest from slow, flaky downstreams.

pushw.name: Push Worker Fleet
pushw.summary: Consumes notif.push from Kafka and calls APNs (iOS) / FCM (Android).

sections.heading: Connection pooling
sections.body: Each worker keeps a persistent HTTP/2 connection per APNs endpoint (production + sandbox) and per FCM project. APNs allows 1000 concurrent streams per connection — one connection can send thousands of pushes/sec.

sections.heading: Device routing
sections.body: Worker resolves (user_id, platform) → device_token(s) from a device-registry cache. A user with 3 devices creates 3 push tasks, sent in parallel.

sections.heading: Collapse keys
sections.body: APNs/FCM support a collapse-id so a burst of updates to the same notification replaces the previous one on the device (saves battery).

sections.heading: Retry policy
sections.body: 5xx from APNs/FCM → republish to `notif.retry` with a scheduled delivery time. 4xx (BadDeviceToken, Unregistered) → mark device invalid and stop retrying.

bottlenecks.title: APNs HTTP/2 connection pool exhaustion at 80K pushes/sec sustained
bottlenecks.trigger: Sustained 80K/sec (0.7 × 115K) push rate with APNs p50 latency of 80ms requires ~6.4K concurrent streams (Little's Law: 80K × 0.08s). During an APNs slowdown where latency jumps from 80ms to 500ms, in-flight demand jumps 6x to ~40K concurrent streams, exceeding the worker fleet's provisioned 5000 concurrency slot budget. With 200 workers × 5 connections × 1000 streams = 1M slots theoretically, but per-worker GOAWAY frames from APNs during maintenance events drop individual connections, and JWT token refresh (required every 55min) can momentarily halve effective capacity.
bottlenecks.symptom: Consumer lag on notif.push grows rapidly (>1M records) while workers show idle CPU — they are blocked on HTTP/2 flow-control. APNs returns GOAWAY or 429 'TooManyRequests'; p99 send latency climbs from 150ms to 2-5s. Transactional pushes (2FA, order-shipped) violate the minute-scale SLO. Retry queue fills with timeouts, amplifying load on recovery.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Run 2x connection headroom (10 connections per worker instead of 5) with staggered JWT refresh windows across the fleet (no more than 10% of workers refreshing simultaneously). Implement per-connection stream-count governor that caps in-flight at 800/connection (20% headroom below APNs' 1000 limit). Use HPA scaling on `kafka_consumer_lag > 1M` to add workers before saturation. For APNs slowdowns, circuit-break to notif.retry after 5s timeouts rather than holding streams open indefinitely.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `apns_concurrent_streams / apns_max_streams > 0.8` per connection for 30s; `kafka_consumer_lag{topic="notif.push"} > 500000` for 2min; `apns_goaway_received_total` spike; p99 send latency > 500ms for 1min; JWT refresh failure rate > 0.

bottlenecks.title: Stale device tokens causing silent drops and bounce amplification
bottlenecks.trigger: At 80K push/sec, even 1% stale device tokens (from app uninstalls, OS token rotation, cache-invalidation pub/sub drops) = 800 BadDeviceToken 4xx/sec = 70M wasted calls/day. Each 4xx still consumes an HTTP/2 stream for ~50ms and a log-write slot, plus a DB write to mark device invalid. During major iOS releases when token churn spikes 10x, 8K/sec of 4xx traffic competes with legitimate deliveries for worker concurrency (budget 5000).
bottlenecks.symptom: APNs `BadDeviceToken` / `Unregistered` response rate climbs above 1% baseline to 5-10%. Users report 'I'm not getting pushes anymore' while log shows status=sent on stale tokens and status=failed with BadDeviceToken on the right-hand device. Worker fleet CPU elevated but effective delivery rate drops. Cache invalidation lag metric pegs above 30s. Device-registry DB sees write amplification as workers bulk-mark tokens invalid.
bottlenecks.mitigation: On every 4xx BadDeviceToken/Unregistered response, synchronously DEL the `dev:{user_id}` cache entry AND mark device row invalid in DB in one transaction — don't rely solely on pub/sub. Negative-cache invalid tokens in worker-local LRU for 60s to avoid immediate re-attempt on the same token across consumer rebalances. After iOS/Android major releases, pre-warm a token-refresh sweep job. Cap devices-per-user at 20 at the device registry to bound worst-case fanout per notification.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `apns_bad_device_token_rate / apns_send_rate > 0.5%` for 5min; `fcm_unregistered_rate > 0.5%`; daily reconciliation job comparing cache-sourced token count vs DB-registered count per user; spike in `device_invalidation_writes_per_sec` above 500.

bottlenecks.title: Per-user ordering head-of-line blocking on partition rebalance
bottlenecks.trigger: notif.push keys by user_id across 200 partitions to preserve per-user ordering (order-confirmed before order-shipped). During a worker deploy or autoscale event, Kafka consumer group rebalance pauses all 200 partitions for 3-10s while partition assignments shuffle. At 80K/sec baseline, 5s of pause = 400K records backed up, concentrated on the resumed partitions. Multi-device users (3 devices each) amplify: one slow APNs response to device 1 blocks device 2 and 3 sends for the same user if the worker processes sequentially to maintain order.
bottlenecks.symptom: Sawtooth pattern on consumer lag — spikes of 300-500K every deploy, slowly draining over 30-60s. Transactional push p99 latency during rebalance windows hits 10-30s. Some partitions permanently skew hotter (power users, viral content) while peers idle; one or two workers pinned at 100% CPU with lag, rest idle.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Switch to Kafka's cooperative-sticky assignor (incremental rebalance) to avoid stop-the-world pauses. Process devices for the same user concurrently with `asyncio.gather` — ordering is preserved at the record level, not within a record's device list. For broadcast traffic, override key to notification_id (not user_id) since per-user ordering is meaningless in a marketing blast. Bump partition count to 400 to halve per-partition worst-case load.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `kafka_consumer_rebalance_duration_ms > 5000`; `kafka_consumer_lag` max/avg ratio > 3x indicating partition skew; per-worker CPU stddev across the fleet > 40%; `apns_send_latency_p99` bumps correlated with deploy markers.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Push Worker Fleet exists here For a notification system handling **10B notifications/day** across three channels, something has to actually pull messages off Kafka and make the HTTPS call to APNs (Apple) or FCM (Google). The Notification API can't do this itself — it accepted the request in 10ms and returned 202 so the producer wasn't blocked. The push workers are the component that does the slow, failure-prone work of talking to Apple and Google: holding persistent HTTP/2 connections, refreshing JWT auth tokens every 55 minutes, resolving which devices a user has, handling partial failures when one of a user's three devices returns `BadDeviceToken`, and deciding whether a 5xx response means "retry in 1 minute" or "this token is dead, stop trying." ## What happens without it If the API called APNs directly, every "your order shipped" request would block for 30–150ms waiting on Apple. During an APNs brownout, API threads would pile up holding open TLS connections, the thread pool would exhaust, and *unrelated* traffic — password reset emails, 2FA SMS — would also start failing because the API itself is unresponsive. Operators would see a global 503 spike; users would miss 2FA codes even though Twilio is perfectly healthy. The queue + worker split isolates Apple's problems to the push lane only. ## The scale math Push is **70% of 115K/sec = ~80K pushes/sec sustained**. At 100ms per APNs call, Little's Law says you need ~8,000 concurrent in-flight calls (80,000 × 0.1s). The design runs ~16 workers at 500 concurrency each = 8,000 slots — exactly sized to the arithmetic, with HTTP/2 multiplexing making each TCP connection carry up to 1,000 of those concurrent streams. ## Trade-off Splitting workers out adds a deployment tier and Kafka consumer-group coordination to operate, but it's the only way one flaky gateway doesn't take down the other two channels.

smsw.name: SMS Worker Fleet
smsw.summary: Consumes notif.sms and submits messages through Twilio / Sinch.

sections.heading: Throughput constraints
sections.body: Carrier-level message rate limits are the binding constraint. Twilio long codes default to 1 msg/sec per number; short codes ~100/sec; toll-free ~3/sec. Scaling means adding numbers or moving to 10DLC/short codes.

sections.heading: Number pool
sections.body: Worker picks a sending number from a pool for the recipient's country. Sticky: the same user always gets the same sender number (carrier filters don't like rotating senders).

sections.heading: Cost & retry
sections.body: SMS is expensive (~$0.01 per message in US). Aggressive retries burn budget — cap retries at 3 and do NOT retry on PERMANENT codes (invalid number, landline).

bottlenecks.title: Carrier per-number throughput ceiling at 11.5K SMS/sec
bottlenecks.trigger: Target load is 10% of 115K/sec = 11.5K SMS/sec sustained. Twilio long codes deliver 1 msg/sec per number, short codes ~100/sec, toll-free ~3/sec. A pool of 200 short codes caps at 20K/sec theoretical but realistic carrier filtering cuts effective throughput 30-50%. During a broadcast adding SMS (e.g., 20M users), offered load can hit 30-50K/sec for minutes, 3-5x pool capacity.
bottlenecks.symptom: notif.sms consumer lag grows unbounded — 1M+ records queued within minutes. Twilio returns HTTP 429 'Too Many Requests' on oversubscribed numbers; worker fleet CPU is idle while records sit in Kafka. Transactional SMS (2FA, password reset) queue behind campaign traffic, blowing the minute-scale SLO — users report 'didn't get my code' and retry, amplifying load. Carrier filters flag sender numbers as spam, degrading delivery for all traffic on shared numbers.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Provision number pool for 2x peak: for 11.5K/sec sustained use at least 150 short codes (100/sec each = 15K/sec ceiling) per country. Partition the pool by criticality — reserve 20% exclusively for transactional traffic with a dedicated notif.sms.transactional topic and worker group, so campaign bursts can't starve 2FA. Move high-volume US traffic to 10DLC registered brands (higher TPS). Implement per-number token buckets in-worker to smooth submits under carrier caps.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `twilio_429_rate > 1%` for 1min per number-pool; `kafka_consumer_lag{topic="notif.sms"} > 500000` for 2min; per-number throughput dashboard flagging any number at >80% of its TPS cap for 5min; separate transactional-vs-campaign lag metrics with PagerDuty on transactional lag > 30s.

bottlenecks.title: Cost blowout from retries and duplicate sends
bottlenecks.trigger: SMS is ~$0.01/msg in US. At 11.5K/sec = ~1B SMS/day ≈ $10M/day baseline spend. A Twilio brownout returning ambiguous 5xx (timeout after submit) causes workers to retry; without strict idempotency on provider_msg_id, a 1% double-send = $100K/day waste. Cap of 3 retries × 11.5K/sec × 1% permanent-failure misclassification = 3.5K wasted sends/sec = ~$30K/day on dead numbers.
bottlenecks.symptom: Finance raises alarm on daily Twilio invoice spiking 20-30%. User complaints: 'I got the same 2FA code 4 times.' Twilio dashboard shows elevated error codes 30003 (unreachable) and 30005 (unknown destination) being retried repeatedly. Post-incident audit of notif_attempts table shows multiple status='sent' rows per notification_id to the same phone.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce strict retry classifier: only retry on transient codes (20429, 20500, network timeout); NEVER retry on 21211 (invalid number), 21610 (unsubscribed), 30003/30005 (permanent). Cap retries at 3 with exponential backoff. Before each submit, check provider-side idempotency by hashing (user_id, template_id, variables) and passing as Twilio's Idempotency-Key header. Pre-flight phone numbers against Twilio Lookup API and cache results 30 days to reject invalid numbers before spending on a send. Daily spend budget with auto-pause of campaign traffic at 120% of baseline.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `sms_cost_per_hour > 1.2 * rolling_7d_avg`; metric `sms_retry_rate_by_error_code` with alarm on permanent-code retries > 0; dedupe audit job comparing distinct notification_ids vs total SMS submitted per day — divergence > 0.1% pages. Twilio webhook feeds status callbacks into log for per-msg-id verification.

bottlenecks.title: Sticky-sender number state blowing worker memory and rebalance cost
bottlenecks.trigger: Sticky sender rule: same user always gets same sender number (carrier filter friendliness). With 1B+ users and 200 numbers per country × 5 countries = 1000 numbers, the (user_id → number) mapping is 1B rows × ~20B = 20GB. If held in worker memory per replica, a 50-worker fleet uses 1TB RAM; if held in shared Redis, every send adds a lookup on the hot path (1-3ms × 11.5K/sec = 11.5K ops/sec per region on a dedicated shard). Consumer group rebalances on deploy reshuffle partitions, invalidating in-worker caches and causing cold-miss storms.
bottlenecks.symptom: Worker memory OOMs during peak if using in-memory map; Redis shard holding sender-assignment hits >80K ops/sec and p99 climbs to 10ms+, stretching SMS worker service time past the 100-400ms envelope. Post-deploy SMS latency p99 spikes for 2-3min while caches rewarm. Occasionally a user's assigned number gets filtered/rotated and the sticky mapping sends them to a blocked number — delivery fails silently.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Store sender assignment in a sharded Redis cluster keyed by hash(user_id) with 60-day TTL, sized for 2x peak QPS (20K ops/sec × 5 regions = 100K capacity, 10+ shards). Use consistent hashing (`sender = pool[hash(user_id) % pool_size]`) as a deterministic default — no state needed, only store overrides for users whose default was filtered. On Kafka rebalance use cooperative-sticky assignor to minimize partition shuffling. Automate pool rotation: when a number is flagged by carrier (via Twilio status callback 30007), evict and remap affected users via background job.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `redis_sender_assignment_ops_per_sec > 80000` or p99 > 5ms; `sms_worker_memory_rss > 80%` of pod limit; `twilio_carrier_filtered_rate per_number > baseline_2x` identifies numbers needing rotation; post-deploy latency SLO (p99 < 500ms for 5min after rebalance) with auto-rollback.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the SMS Worker Fleet is here For a notification system at 10B/day, SMS is the most *operationally weird* of the three channels. Unlike push (where Apple accepts thousands of concurrent HTTP/2 streams per connection) or email (where SendGrid handles throughput for you), SMS throughput is gated by **carrier rules on each sending phone number** — a Twilio long code sends 1 msg/sec, a short code ~100/sec. You can't just "scale up" by adding servers; you have to manage a *pool of phone numbers* and route each user stickily to the same sender number so carriers don't flag you as spam. That logic doesn't belong in the generic API layer — it's SMS-specific, so it lives in a dedicated worker fleet consuming `notif.sms`. ## What happens without it If the Notification API called Twilio directly, a single 2FA burst would exhaust the 1-msg/sec-per-number budget, Twilio would return 429s, and the API would either block (starving other channels) or drop the SMS entirely. Worse, since SMS is ~$0.01/message, a naive retry loop on a malformed phone number could burn thousands of dollars in minutes. The operator would see Twilio spend spike on the invoice while users complain they never got their login codes. ## The scale math SMS is 10% of 115K/sec = **11,500 SMS/sec sustained**. At 100/sec per short code, that requires a pool of at least 115 short codes — realistically 150+ with headroom. The worker fleet is what actually *routes* each message to the right number from that pool, tracks per-number throughput, and respects the carrier ceiling. ## Trade-off Isolating SMS into its own fleet means more deployment units to operate, but it's the only way carrier throughput limits don't bleed into push and email.

emailw.name: Email Worker Fleet
emailw.summary: Consumes notif.email and submits via SendGrid / SES / Postmark.

sections.heading: Delivery path
sections.body: Worker renders the template (variables → HTML + text parts), attaches headers (List-Unsubscribe, Feedback-ID), and POSTs to the provider's v3 API. The provider handles MTA, DKIM, SPF, bounce tracking.

sections.heading: Suppression list
sections.body: Before sending, worker checks a suppression-list cache for hard-bounces and unsubscribes. Sending to a suppressed address is a compliance violation.

sections.heading: Warmup
sections.body: New IPs/domains need 2-4 weeks of gradually increasing volume to build sender reputation. Mass blasts from a cold IP go to spam.

bottlenecks.title: Provider API throughput and connection pool saturation at 23K emails/sec
bottlenecks.trigger: Email is 20% of 115K/sec = 23K emails/sec sustained. At p50 provider latency of 150ms, Little's Law requires ~3.5K concurrent in-flight requests (23K × 0.15s) — right at the worker fleet's 2000 concurrency budget. During SendGrid/SES API slowdowns (latency climbing to 500ms-1s), concurrent demand jumps to 12-23K, 6-10x over budget. Provider per-account rate limits (SendGrid Pro: ~10K req/s per subuser; SES: 200 req/s default, raises to ~1K) also cap sustainable throughput unless traffic is sharded across subusers/accounts.
bottlenecks.symptom: notif.email consumer lag grows rapidly (millions of records queued within minutes). Worker CPU is idle while connections block on provider ACKs. Provider returns 429 'rate limit exceeded' or 503s; worker fleet circuit-breaks and floods notif.retry. Transactional email (password reset, receipts) queues behind campaign traffic, violating the minute-scale SLO — users report 'never got my password reset link' and retry, amplifying load.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shard traffic across 5+ SendGrid subusers (or SES configuration sets) keyed by hash(user_id) for ~50K/sec aggregate headroom (2x peak). Provision 2000 persistent HTTP/2 connections with request multiplexing across the fleet (~50 workers × 40 connections). Separate transactional and campaign traffic onto distinct notif.email.transactional and notif.email.campaign topics with dedicated worker groups and subusers so bursts can't starve transactional. Implement per-subuser token buckets in-worker to stay under provider TPS caps. Use HPA scaling on kafka_consumer_lag > 500K.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `sendgrid_429_rate > 0.5%` for 1min per subuser; `kafka_consumer_lag{topic="notif.email"} > 500000` for 2min; provider API latency p99 > 500ms for 1min; per-subuser TPS dashboard flagging any subuser at >80% of cap; separate transactional lag SLO (p99 < 30s) with PagerDuty.

bottlenecks.title: Suppression-list cache staleness causing compliance violations
bottlenecks.trigger: Every send must check the suppression list for hard-bounces, spam complaints, and unsubscribes before hitting the provider. At 23K/sec with a suppression list of 100M+ entries (typical for a mature 1B-user system), the cache is the hot path. A Redis failover, pub/sub drop from the webhook ingestion pipeline, or stale TTL means unsubscribe signals take minutes to propagate. At 23K/sec even a 60-second lag = 1.4M emails sent through a window where users may have unsubscribed, and 0.01% compliance miss = 2.3 violations/sec = ~200K/day.
bottlenecks.symptom: Provider dashboards (SendGrid/SES) show rising spam-complaint rate crossing the 0.1% threshold — triggering provider-side reputation drops and temporary send holds. Legal/compliance team receives CAN-SPAM or GDPR complaints. ISP filters (Gmail, Yahoo) mark domain as spam, causing campaign delivery to drop to inbox rates <50%. Post-incident audit shows emails sent to addresses on the suppression list after the unsubscribe timestamp.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Write-through cache on suppression: webhook handler updates both DB and Redis synchronously in one transaction, not via async pub/sub. Use short TTL (60s max) on positive 'not-suppressed' cache entries; permanent/long TTL on suppression hits (fail-safe: err toward not-sending). Add a worker-local bloom filter of all suppressed addresses (100M entries × 10 bits = 125MB per worker) as a fast first-pass with Redis fallback on filter hit. Daily reconciliation job comparing sent-emails vs suppression-DB to catch divergence.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `sendgrid_spam_complaint_rate > 0.05%` (half of the 0.1% provider threshold) for 1h; `suppression_cache_miss_rate > 1%` for 30s; webhook ingestion lag > 30s; daily reconciliation job pages if any sent-after-suppressed rows found; domain reputation monitor (Google Postmaster, SNDS) for sudden drops.

bottlenecks.title: IP/domain reputation collapse from campaign bursts on warming pool
bottlenecks.trigger: New sending IPs require 2-4 weeks of gradually increasing volume (typically starting at a few thousand/day and doubling) to build reputation. During a 100M-user broadcast at 23K/sec, the fleet may exceed the warmed IP pool's capacity and spill onto cold/partially-warmed IPs — or exceed per-IP hourly caps set by major ISPs (Gmail, Yahoo, Outlook each enforce throttles like 10-100K/hr per new IP). Broadcasts of 100M recipients / 50 warmed IPs = 2M per IP — far beyond a warming IP's daily budget.
bottlenecks.symptom: Campaign delivery rate to Gmail/Yahoo drops from ~95% inbox to <50% (spam folder) within hours. ISPs return 421 'too many connections' or 4.7.0 'rate limited' soft-bounces; provider retries with backoff, causing notif.retry to swell with millions of bounced emails. Marketing sees open rates crater post-campaign. Restoring reputation takes weeks — during which all email campaigns are degraded.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce per-IP daily send budgets at the worker (e.g., new IP: 10K/day, week 2: 50K/day, steady state: 1M/day) with a scheduler that round-robins warmed IPs and refuses to spill to cold ones. Pre-plan broadcast launches 2-4 weeks ahead with a warming schedule that ramps total pool capacity. Segregate transactional (established, high-reputation IPs) and marketing (warming pool) onto separate dedicated IP pools — never mix. Throttle per-ISP using feedback from bounce codes (if Gmail soft-bounces, back off for that ISP specifically).
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor Google Postmaster Tools and Microsoft SNDS daily for domain/IP reputation scores; alert on any IP dropping to 'Medium' or below. Alert on `isp_softbounce_rate{isp="gmail"} > 2%` for 10min; per-IP daily send count dashboard with hard cap alarms; campaign pre-flight check that refuses to launch if recipients/warmed_capacity > 1.0.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Email Worker Fleet exists here For a notification system at 10B/day across three channels, email has its own set of operational headaches that don't apply to push or SMS. Every email send needs to check a **suppression list** (hard-bounces, unsubscribes — sending to these is a CAN-SPAM or GDPR violation), **render HTML + plain-text parts**, attach compliance headers like `List-Unsubscribe`, and go out through a sending IP that has built up **reputation over weeks of gradual warmup**. None of that belongs in the generic API layer or in the push workers — it's email-specific logic, so it lives in a dedicated fleet consuming `notif.email`. ## What happens without it If the API called SendGrid directly, a burst of password-reset emails would block API threads for 50–250ms each, the thread pool would exhaust, and push + SMS would also start failing — even though Apple and Twilio are perfectly healthy. Worse, without a worker-side suppression check, a marketing blast could hit 100K unsubscribed users, trigger spam complaints above the 0.1% ISP threshold, and tank your domain reputation. Operators would see Gmail delivery drop from 95% inbox to <50% spam folder, and recovering takes *weeks*. ## The scale math Email is 20% of 115K/sec = **23K emails/sec sustained**. At a provider p50 latency of 150ms, Little's Law says you need 23,000 × 0.15 = **~3,450 concurrent in-flight requests**. The fleet is provisioned at 2,000 concurrency across ~50 workers with a pool of ~2K persistent HTTP connections — tight enough that a provider slowdown to 500ms latency (jumping demand to 11,500 concurrent) is a real bottleneck the design has to plan around. ## Trade-off Isolating email into its own fleet means a third deployment tier to operate, but it's the only way suppression checks and IP warmup budgets stay scoped to email without leaking into push or SMS logic.

gateway.name: External Gateways (APNs / FCM / Twilio / SendGrid)
gateway.summary: Grouped abstraction for the 3rd-party services that actually deliver to devices / networks.

sections.heading: Why group them
sections.body: They share operational characteristics: TLS HTTP/2 endpoints, per-account throughput quotas, variable latency (~50-500ms), occasional region-wide brownouts. The system should treat them uniformly w.r.t. retry and circuit-breaking.

sections.heading: SLAs worth knowing
sections.body:
- APNs: 99.9% availability; per-connection 1000 concurrent streams; 4KB payload cap
- FCM: similar; priority=high for transactional
- Twilio Programmable Messaging: p99 delivery ~10s, carrier-dependent
- SendGrid: p99 API ack ~500ms; actual inbox arrival minutes-hours depending on provider reputation

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Brownouts — circuit-break for 30s and shed to `notif.retry`
- Token expiry (APNs JWT) — worker must refresh every 55 minutes
- Carrier filter blocks — alert on elevated 4xx from a specific country/number

bottlenecks.title: Regional brownout / provider outage cascading into retry-queue backlog
bottlenecks.trigger: APNs, FCM, Twilio, or SendGrid has a regional brownout (documented 99.9% SLA = ~43min/month of allowed downtime). At 115K/sec total (80K push + 23K email + 11.5K SMS), a 10-minute APNs brownout means ~48M pushes fail and get republished to notif.retry with 1m/5m/30m backoff — creating a thundering herd when the gateway recovers and retries align on minute boundaries.
bottlenecks.symptom: On-call sees apns_timeout_total spiking to >1K/sec, notif.retry lag balloons past 50M records, and post-recovery the push traffic doubles to ~160K/sec as retries merge with live traffic — re-browning out the just-recovered gateway. Transactional push p99 latency stretches from 150ms to minutes, blowing the minute-scale SLO for 2FA and order-shipped notifications.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Implement a per-gateway circuit breaker (e.g., resilience4j) that trips on >50% failures over a 30s window and sheds directly to notif.retry without attempting the gateway call — preventing worker pool exhaustion waiting on timeouts. Add decorrelated jitter to backoff (`delay = base * 2^n * random(0.5, 1.5)`) so retries don't align. Cap retry-to-main republish rate at 20% of main topic capacity (16K/sec for push). Separate transactional and campaign retries onto distinct topics so 2FA doesn't queue behind marketing blasts.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `gateway_circuit_breaker_state{provider=~"apns|fcm|twilio|sendgrid"} == open` for >30s; `rate(gateway_timeout_total[1m]) > 500` per provider; `kafka_consumer_lag{topic="notif.retry"} > 10M`; post-recovery watch on `rate(kafka_producer_send{topic="notif.push",source="retry"}[1m]) > 20000`.

bottlenecks.title: APNs JWT token expiry and HTTP/2 GOAWAY causing synchronized reconnects
bottlenecks.trigger: APNs requires JWT provider tokens refreshed every 55 minutes (hard-rejects tokens older than 1h with 403 ExpiredProviderToken). At 80K push/sec across ~200 workers × 5 connections = 1000 connections, if all workers bootstrap from the same initial token, they expire simultaneously — causing 1000 concurrent reconnects and JWT-signing bursts. APNs also periodically issues GOAWAY frames (server-initiated graceful close) during maintenance, forcing mass reconnection.
bottlenecks.symptom: Every ~55 minutes, push delivery p99 spikes from 150ms to 2-5s for 10-30s as connections tear down and re-establish TLS + HTTP/2 handshakes. 403 ExpiredProviderToken errors flood logs simultaneously across the fleet; consumer lag on notif.push jumps by 500K-1M records during each refresh window. During GOAWAY events, the stream budget (1000/connection) momentarily halves and in-flight requests stall.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Stagger JWT refresh across the fleet: each worker refreshes at `(worker_id % 55) minutes past boot` so no more than 2% of workers refresh in any given minute. Pre-fetch new JWT 5 minutes before expiry and swap atomically without closing the connection (APNs accepts new JWTs on existing connections). Maintain 2x connection headroom (10 per worker) so GOAWAY on one connection leaves 9 active. Use exponential backoff on reconnect with jitter to avoid thundering herd.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `apns_expired_provider_token_total > 10/sec` (should be near-zero with staggered refresh); `apns_goaway_received_total` spikes; `apns_connection_established_total` rate anomaly (should be flat, not bursty); p99 push latency sawtooth pattern at 55-minute intervals visible on dashboards.

bottlenecks.title: Per-account throughput quota ceilings limiting effective delivery rate
bottlenecks.trigger: Each gateway enforces per-account TPS caps that bind below theoretical infrastructure limits: SES default 200 req/s (raises to ~1K), SendGrid Pro ~10K req/s per subuser, Twilio short codes ~100/sec per number, FCM ~1M/min per project. At design targets (23K email/sec, 11.5K SMS/sec, 80K push/sec), a single account/subuser/project saturates quota long before HTTP/2 connection or worker capacity is reached. A misconfigured fleet routing all traffic through one subuser caps at 10K/sec regardless of how many workers are running.
bottlenecks.symptom: Gateway returns HTTP 429 'rate_limit_exceeded' or provider-specific quota errors (SES Throttling, Twilio 20429). Worker fleet CPU is idle while Kafka consumer lag grows; notif.retry fills with 429 retries that will re-fail until quota resets. Finance sees no cost increase but delivery SLOs are missed — a silent degradation. Hot-account problem: one tenant (e.g., marketing subuser) hits quota while others sit at 5%.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shard traffic across ≥5 subusers/projects/accounts per provider, keyed by hash(user_id), to multiply headroom (5x SendGrid subusers = 50K/sec aggregate). Implement per-account token buckets in-worker to pre-throttle and stay under quota (e.g., 80% of cap) rather than relying on gateway 429s. Request quota raises proactively based on 30-day trending (SES supports automatic raises; Twilio requires tickets). Dedicate separate accounts for transactional vs campaign traffic so bursts can't starve 2FA.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `gateway_429_rate{provider=~".*"} > 0.5%` for 1min per-account; per-account TPS dashboard flagging any account at >80% of its documented cap for 5min; `gateway_quota_remaining{provider="ses"} / gateway_quota_limit < 0.2`; separate transactional-vs-campaign 429 rate with PagerDuty on transactional > 0.1%.
