prebuild.explanation: ## Why the external gateways are called out as a component For a notification system delivering 10B messages/day across push, SMS, and email, *you* don't actually deliver anything to a user's phone. Apple owns the pipe to iPhones (APNs), Google owns Android (FCM), carriers own SMS (reached via Twilio/Sinch), and ISPs own email inboxes (reached via SendGrid/SES). The design calls these out as a grouped component because they share a very particular operational profile: they are **slow** (50–500ms per call), **rate-limited per account**, and **occasionally brown out for minutes at a time** — and you have zero control over any of it. Treating them as one abstraction lets the system apply uniform retry, circuit-breaking, and timeout policy. ## What happens without planning for them Imagine APNs has a 10-minute regional brownout. Calls that used to return in 80ms now hang for 30s. If the push workers didn't treat the gateway as an unreliable external dependency, every worker thread would pile up waiting on hung TLS connections, the worker pool would exhaust, Kafka consumer lag on `notif.push` would explode from ~12K to tens of millions, and transactional notifications (2FA codes, order confirmations) would miss the minute-scale SLO. Operators would see APNs timeout metrics spike; users would think *your* app is broken. ## The arithmetic Push traffic is 80K/sec sustained. APNs p50 latency is ~80ms, so by Little's Law you need 80,000 × 0.08 = **6,400 concurrent in-flight streams**. If latency degrades to 500ms during a brownout, concurrent demand jumps to 40,000 — 6× higher. The design provisions 200 workers × 5 connections × 1000 streams = 1M stream slots with circuit-breakers that shed to `notif.retry` after 5s, so a brownout doesn't consume the whole worker fleet. ## The trade-off Accepting that these gateways are unreliable third parties means building retry queues, circuit breakers, and JWT refresh logic — significant complexity — but the alternative (running your own push/SMS/email delivery) is effectively impossible.

log.name: Notification Log DB
log.summary: Append-only record of every notification attempt — status, timestamp, provider response. The book lists this explicitly as a reliability + analytics sink that feeds dashboards and supports auditing 'did X actually get the message?'.

sections.heading: Purpose (book)
sections.body:
Three use cases:
1. Analytics — open rate, click rate, conversion per campaign.
2. Support/debug — 'why didn't user 4782 get the push?' answered from one PK lookup.
3. Compliance — proof-of-send for SMS/email regulatory requirements.

sections.heading: Data model
sections.body:
```
TABLE notif_attempts (Cassandra) notification_id UUID attempt_no INT user_id BIGINT channel TEXT status TEXT ('queued','sent','delivered','failed','suppressed') provider TEXT provider_msg_id TEXT error_code TEXT created_at TIMESTAMP PRIMARY KEY ((notification_id), attempt_no)
```

sections.heading: Query patterns
sections.body:
- GET /v1/notify/:id/status → single-row by notification_id (PK lookup)
- Per-user history: secondary table keyed by user_id, bucketed by day
- Campaign summary: rolled up into analytics store, not queried from this DB directly

sections.heading: Retention
sections.body: Raw attempts kept 90 days for support/troubleshooting; aggregated analytics beyond that.

bottlenecks.title: Write amplification from 10B attempts/day with multi-attempt + multi-device fanout
bottlenecks.trigger: Baseline is 10B notifications/day = ~115K/sec, but the log records one row per attempt per device. Power users with 3 devices × occasional 2nd-attempt retries pushes the effective write rate to ~200-300K rows/sec sustained, and during a 100M broadcast with a 1% retry rate ingestion spikes to ~500K writes/sec. With the budgeted 3000 concurrency and 5-20ms write latency (Little's Law: 3000/0.012s = 250K/sec ceiling), sustained bursts saturate the cluster.
bottlenecks.symptom: Cassandra write latency p99 climbs from 20ms to 200ms+, pending mutations queue grows, hints pile up on coordinators. Workers block on log.write before committing Kafka offsets — consumer lag on notif.push/sms/email grows even though gateways are healthy. On-call sees 'cassandra_MutationStage_PendingTasks > 10000' while CPU is already saturated on write path.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Batch writes at the worker (50-100 rows per BATCH LOGGED statement, grouped by partition key) to amortize coordinator overhead. Scale to 30+ nodes sized for 2x peak write throughput. Use LeveledCompactionStrategy only on read-hot tables; keep notif_attempts on TimeWindowCompactionStrategy (90-day retention, time-series write pattern) to bound compaction IO. Consider async fire-and-forget writes for campaign traffic (accept rare loss) while keeping synchronous LOCAL_QUORUM for transactional.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `cassandra_MutationStage_PendingTasks > 5000` per node for 1min; `cassandra_WriteLatency{table="notif_attempts"}_p99 > 50ms`; worker-side metric `log_write_duration_p99 > 30ms` correlated with Kafka consumer lag growth.

bottlenecks.title: Storage and compaction pressure from 90-day retention × 10B rows/day
bottlenecks.trigger: 10B rows/day × ~300B/row × 90-day retention = ~270TB raw, ~50-90TB after compression. TimeWindowCompactionStrategy with daily windows produces 90 active SSTables per node; adding retries and multi-device fanout pushes this to 600TB+ raw across a 20-node cluster (~30TB/node), crossing the recommended 2-4TB/node density ceiling for Cassandra.
bottlenecks.symptom: Per-node disk utilization crosses 80%, compaction throughput falls behind ingest, SSTables-per-read p99 climbs to 10+, read latency on /v1/notify/:id/status degrades from 5ms to 100ms+. Streaming/bootstrap of a replacement node takes days instead of hours. Repair jobs don't complete within the gc_grace_seconds window (10d default) risking resurrected tombstones.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Tier storage: keep last 7 days on fast NVMe nodes for support lookups, move 8-90 days to cheaper object-store-backed tier (Cassandra tiered storage, or periodic export to S3+Parquet with Athena for audit queries). Enforce per-table TTL (90d) at write time rather than relying on deletes. Scale cluster to 40+ nodes to keep per-node density under 3TB. Evaluate DynamoDB alternative (listed in design) if ops overhead dominates — predictable $/write at this scale may win despite lock-in.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on per-node `disk_used_pct > 70%`; `cassandra_CompactionsPending > 20` for 10min; `cassandra_SSTablesPerReadHistogram_p99 > 8` on notif_attempts; daily capacity-forecasting job projecting disk-full < 14 days ahead.

bottlenecks.title: Hot-partition reads on per-user history secondary table
bottlenecks.trigger: The secondary access pattern 'per-user history keyed by user_id, bucketed by day' creates partition keys like (user_id, date). Power users (internal service accounts, shared family accounts, test users) can receive 1000+ notifications/day, producing oversized partitions. Support queries ('why didn't user X get their push?') issued on these users pull wide partitions, and bots scraping history via the GET /v1/notify/user/:id endpoint amplify load on specific hot partitions.
bottlenecks.symptom: One Cassandra node shows 2-3x CPU vs peers — classic hot-partition signature. Support tool queries time out for specific users while others are fast. `nodetool tablehistograms` shows a single partition in the 99th percentile for partition size (>100MB) and read count. Tombstone-scanned warnings in the logs when the 90d TTL starts expiring rows within the hot partition.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Bucket per-user history by (user_id, date, hour_bucket) or by (user_id, week) to cap partition size; enforce a hard limit of ~10K rows per partition via application-side chunking. Cache recent-history responses (last 7 days) in Redis with a 60s TTL to absorb support-tool read spikes. Rate-limit the /user/:id history endpoint to 10 req/sec per caller. Move power-user/service-account traffic to a separate keyspace with wider bucketing.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-node CPU skew alert (`max(cpu)/avg(cpu) > 2`); `nodetool tablehistograms notif_attempts_by_user` flagging partitions > 50MB; `cassandra_TombstoneScannedHistogram_p99 > 1000` indicating wide-partition TTL churn; API-side metric on history-endpoint p99 latency > 500ms.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why there's a separate log for every notification attempt For a notification system at 10B messages/day, three questions come up constantly and none of them can be answered from Kafka or the live user DB: *"Did user 4782 actually get their password reset email?"* (support), *"What's our delivery rate on Android today?"* (analytics), and *"Prove to this regulator that we sent the SMS consent confirmation on March 3rd"* (compliance). The Notification Log is the append-only record that makes all three answerable. Every time a worker calls APNs, Twilio, or SendGrid and gets back a response — success, 4xx, timeout — it writes one row here with the provider's message ID and error code. Kafka can't serve this: its records age out at 7 days and you can't query them by `user_id` or `notification_id`. ## What breaks without it A user emails support: *"I never got my 2FA code."* Without the log, the operator has no way to distinguish *"we never sent it"* from *"Twilio accepted it but the carrier dropped it"* from *"it was sent to a phone number the user changed last week."* They'd have to guess. Meanwhile, marketing can't tell if a campaign actually reached its 100M users or quietly failed at 40%. ## The scale math At 10B notifications/day × ~300 bytes/row = **3 TB/day of writes**, or ~115K row-inserts/sec sustained. That's why the design picks Cassandra (or DynamoDB) — a relational DB would choke on a write rate that high with 90-day retention (~270 TB raw). ## Trade-off You're paying real storage cost and an extra write on the hot path to buy observability, audit trails, and the ability to actually debug delivery failures — which at this scale is non-negotiable.

analytics.name: Analytics (OLAP / Dashboards)
analytics.summary: Stream processor that aggregates notification outcomes for dashboards and alerting.

sections.heading: Pipeline
sections.body: Flink job consumes from a CDC stream on the notification log and computes rolling aggregates: delivery rate by channel, p95 latency, provider error breakdown, campaign conversion.

sections.heading: Outputs
sections.body:
- Druid / ClickHouse for interactive dashboards
- PagerDuty alerts on delivery rate drops > 5%
- Per-campaign CSVs for marketing

sections.heading: Why async
sections.body: Delivery hot path must not block on analytics. Slight lag (seconds-minutes) is fine.

bottlenecks.title: CDC stream ingest lag at 115K events/sec sustained, 500K/sec during broadcasts
bottlenecks.trigger: The Flink job consumes a CDC stream from the notification log, which writes ~115K rows/sec baseline and spikes to 300-500K/sec during a 100M broadcast fanout (multi-device + multi-attempt amplification). The component's budgeted concurrency of 500 with 20-100ms per-event service time gives a Little's-Law ceiling of ~25K events/sec per Flink task — a single-parallelism job saturates at ~5x below sustained load, and broadcast bursts push 10-20x over budget.
bottlenecks.symptom: Flink job consumer lag on the CDC topic grows from seconds to 10+ minutes; dashboards show stale delivery-rate numbers (marketing sees '40% delivered' when reality is 95%); the 'delivery rate drop >5%' PagerDuty alert either fires late (incident already resolved) or fails to fire because windowed aggregates haven't flushed. Checkpoint duration climbs past the checkpoint interval, causing backpressure and eventual job restart loops.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Scale Flink parallelism to match CDC partition count (e.g., 200 parallel subtasks matching notif_attempts CDC partitions), keyBy(channel, minute_bucket) for even distribution. Use RocksDB state backend with incremental checkpoints (10s interval, 60s timeout). Pre-aggregate at source with a 1-second tumbling pre-window to reduce downstream cardinality 60x before the main 1-minute window. Size Flink TaskManagers for 3x peak (1.5M events/sec headroom) so broadcast bursts don't trigger restart storms.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `flink_job_consumer_lag_seconds > 60` for 2min; `flink_checkpoint_duration_ms > flink_checkpoint_interval_ms * 0.8`; `flink_backpressure_ratio > 0.5` on any operator; dashboard freshness metric (`now - max(metrics.delivery_rate.window_end)`) paging at >90s staleness.

bottlenecks.title: Druid/ClickHouse ingestion and query contention at 10B rows/day
bottlenecks.trigger: At 10B notifications/day with multi-attempt fanout, the analytics OLAP store ingests ~300K rows/sec sustained into per-channel, per-provider, per-campaign rollups. During a 100M broadcast, marketing dashboards issue high-cardinality interactive queries (group by campaign_id, 1-minute buckets, last 24h = 1440 buckets × 100s of campaigns) against the same segments being actively ingested — contending for the same disk IO and query threadpool.
bottlenecks.symptom: Dashboard p95 query latency climbs from 500ms to 10-30s during peak campaign hours; marketing reports 'the campaign dashboard is broken' mid-launch. ClickHouse/Druid shows elevated `MergeTree` parts count (>300 per partition, threshold 150) causing read amplification. Per-campaign CSV exports time out at the 60s HTTP limit. Ingestion lag grows as queries starve the merge/compaction threadpool.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Separate ingest and query clusters via ClickHouse replicas (writes to leader, reads from followers) or Druid historical vs middle-manager separation. Pre-aggregate hot dashboard queries via materialized views (per-minute rollups by channel/provider/campaign) so interactive queries hit <1000 rows instead of millions. Tier data: last 24h on NVMe hot tier, 7-90d on S3/object-store cold tier with query federation. Enforce a query concurrency limit (max 20 concurrent dashboard queries) with a queue; reject/queue CSV exports to an off-peak batch job.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `clickhouse_query_duration_p95 > 5s` for 5min; `clickhouse_parts_per_partition > 200`; `druid_segment_scan_pending > 100`; ingestion lag `ingest_rows_behind > 5_000_000`; per-campaign CSV export failure rate > 1%.

bottlenecks.title: Alerting false negatives during Flink job restart windows
bottlenecks.trigger: The 'delivery rate drop >5%' PagerDuty alert is computed from windowed Flink aggregates. When the Flink job restarts (deploy, OOM, checkpoint failure, or backpressure-induced task failure), recovery from the last checkpoint takes 30s-5min depending on state size (RocksDB with 24h of per-campaign state can be 10s of GB). During recovery, no aggregates are emitted, so the alert rule evaluates on stale or missing data and silently passes — masking an actual gateway brownout that would otherwise page.
bottlenecks.symptom: Post-incident review finds that APNs was browning out for 8 minutes at 15% failure rate but no delivery-rate alert fired — because Flink was recovering from a checkpoint during those minutes. On-call discovered the brownout only via raw `apns_timeout_total` counter from the push-worker fleet. SLO burn-rate dashboards show gaps. Trust in the analytics-driven alerting erodes.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Never rely solely on windowed stream-processor output for critical alerts. Run alert rules in two places: (1) the stream-aggregate path for rich per-campaign/per-channel breakdowns, and (2) a direct Prometheus counter path (`rate(apns_timeout_total[5m]) / rate(apns_send_total[5m]) > 0.05`) scraped from the push-worker fleet for a backstop. Add a 'Flink job health' meta-alert (`flink_job_uptime_seconds < 300` or `flink_checkpoints_completed_total not increasing`) that pages when analytics is itself down, so operators know to fall back to raw metrics. Size checkpoint state to recover in <60s.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `flink_job_uptime_seconds < 300` indicating recent restart; `absent(metrics_delivery_rate{channel="push"}[2m])` catching missing-data silence; checkpoint failure rate `rate(flink_checkpoint_failed_total[10m]) > 0`; reconciliation job comparing Flink-emitted send counts vs raw Cassandra COUNT(*) per hour — divergence >1% indicates missed events.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why there's a separate analytics pipeline For a notification system pushing 10B messages/day, three groups of people constantly need to know *what actually happened*: marketing ("did my 100M-user campaign land?"), on-call engineers ("is push delivery degrading right now?"), and product managers ("what's our open rate by channel this week?"). The raw Notification Log in Cassandra stores every attempt, but it's optimized for single-row lookups by `notification_id` — not for "group by campaign, bucket by minute, over the last 24 hours." That's a completely different query shape, and running it against Cassandra would crush the same cluster that workers are writing 115K rows/sec into. So the design splits reads: Cassandra owns point lookups, while Flink + Druid/ClickHouse own aggregations. ## What breaks without it Imagine APNs is browning out and push delivery drops to 70%. Without a streaming aggregator, nobody notices for 30 minutes — until support tickets pile up. Meanwhile, a marketing team launches a campaign and has no live dashboard, so they can't tell if their 100M blast actually reached users or silently failed at partition 87. The operator ends up running ad-hoc `SELECT COUNT(*)` queries against Cassandra, which slows down the hot write path and makes things worse. ## The scale math At 115K notification attempts/sec sustained, a 1-minute tumbling window processes **6.9M events per window**. Flink's stream-processing model handles that at ~20–100ms per event with 500 concurrency — where an OLTP database would choke. ## Trade-off Dashboards lag reality by seconds to minutes, but that's fine because analytics must never block delivery on the hot path.

operations.title: Send single push notification (happy path)
operations.name: Send single push notification (happy path)
operations.description: A transactional push (e.g. 'your order shipped') — API accepts, queues, push worker consumes and calls APNs, log is updated.

steps.title: App server fires transactional notification
steps.action: The commerce service finishes marking the order as shipped and POSTs a notification request to the Notification API with an idempotency key.

steps.title: Notification server validates request
steps.action: Server checks the Idempotency-Key for dedupe, confirms the template exists, and binds variables. Needs to fetch template + user settings + device tokens next.

steps.title: Cache returns template + device tokens + user settings
steps.action: Redis MGET on three hot keys. Hits on all three — template was warmed at deploy time; device tokens for user 4782 were cached on login; user settings were cached on last notification.

steps.title: Server checks opt-in + quiet hours
steps.action: Push is enabled for this user and we're outside their quiet hours. Proceed to rate limiter.
steps.codeOrCommand:
if not settings.push_enabled: return 204
if settings.in_quiet_hours(now): defer_until = settings.quiet_end

steps.title: Rate limiter grants a token
steps.action: Redis Lua script atomically checks the bucket for (user=4782, channel=push). The user has sent 2 pushes in the last minute — under the limit of 10.
steps.codeOrCommand:
EVAL "local k='rl:push:4782'
local n=redis.call('INCR',k)
if n==1 then redis.call('EXPIRE',k,60) end
if n>10 then return 0 end
return 1" 0

steps.title: API writes to Kafka (notif.push)
steps.action: API assigns a notification_id (UUIDv7) and produces to notif.push with key=user_id for per-user ordering.

steps.title: Kafka persists to partition 87
steps.action: hash(4782) mod 200 = 87. The record is appended to partition 87 with acks=all — leader + at least one replica ack before returning.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# Broker-side
TOPIC notif.push PARTITION 87 OFFSET 4832921 key = '4782' value = {"nid":"01HWR...",...} ack = all (2/3 ISR)

steps.title: API returns 202 to producer
steps.action: API returns immediately with the notification_id. Actual delivery continues asynchronously.
steps.codeOrCommand:
return 202, { "notification_id": "01HWR...", "status": "queued"
}

steps.title: Push worker polls and picks up the record
steps.action: A push-worker consumer in group 'pushw-prod' fetches the batch from partition 87. It resolves user 4782's device_tokens from the device cache — 2 devices (iPhone + iPad).
steps.codeOrCommand: for rec in consumer.poll(timeout_ms=200): devs = device_cache.get(rec.user_id) # [{token:'aXb...', platform:'apns'}, {token:'cYd...', platform:'apns'}] body = render(rec.template_id, rec.variables) # {'aps': {'alert': 'Your order #9921 ships Friday'}} for d in devs: gateway.send_async(d, body, collapse_id=f'ord-{rec.variables.order_id}')

steps.title: APNs delivers to both devices
steps.action: Worker holds a persistent HTTP/2 connection to api.push.apple.com. Two POSTs on two streams; both return:status 200 in ~80ms.
steps.codeOrCommand:
POST /3/device/aXb... HTTP/2
apns-topic: com.example.app
apns-push-type: alert
apns-collapse-id: ord-9921
authorization: bearer <jwt> {"aps":{"alert":"Your order #9921 ships Friday"}} # Response:status: 200
apns-id: 8A2C9F9E-...

steps.title: Worker records attempt outcome
steps.action: A single row per device per attempt is written to notif_attempts. Status 'sent' reflects APNs accepted the message — actual device delivery is not acknowledged back.
steps.codeOrCommand:
INSERT INTO notif_attempts (notification_id, attempt_no, user_id, channel, status, provider, provider_msg_id, created_at)
VALUES ('01HWR...', 1, 4782, 'push', 'sent', 'apns', '8A2C9F9E-...', now);

steps.title: Worker commits Kafka offset
steps.action: After the terminal status is logged, the consumer commits offset 4832922 for partition 87. If the worker crashed before this, another worker would re-deliver — idempotency key protects against double-send at the provider level (collapse_id + dedupe).
steps.codeOrCommand: consumer.commit({('notif.push', 87): 4832922})

steps.title: Analytics ingests outcome (async)
steps.action: CDC stream from the notification log flows into Flink, which updates the per-minute 'push delivery rate' metric on the dashboard.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# Flink
attempts.keyBy('channel').window(Tumbling(1m)).aggregate(DeliveryRate).to('ck://metrics.delivery_rate')

operations.title: Bulk broadcast (100M-user fanout)
operations.name: Bulk broadcast (100M-user fanout)
operations.description: A marketing campaign sends one push to 100M users. API fans out into per-user records; Kafka absorbs the burst; workers drain over ~10 minutes.

steps.title: Campaign tool POSTs a broadcast request
steps.action: The marketing console submits a segment (100M user_ids) and a template. The API endpoint is /v1/notify/broadcast — different route, higher rate limit, requires admin role.

steps.title: API schedules fanout job
steps.action: Instead of fanning out inline (100M DB reads on the request thread — bad), the API enqueues a fanout job and returns a broadcast_id. A dedicated fanout worker pool reads the segment from the user store in chunks.
steps.note: This step exists because inline fanout of 100M would blow the API's memory and timeouts. Two-stage fanout is the standard pattern (, 'News Feed' ).

steps.title: Fanout worker batch-produces 100M records
steps.action: A fanout job pulls user_ids from the segment store 10K at a time and produces to notif.push. Kafka absorbs the burst easily (peak ~200K/sec per topic). Total produce time ≈ 100M / 200K = 500s (~8 min).

steps.title: Push workers scale horizontally
steps.action: With 200 partitions on notif.push and 200 workers × 500 concurrent pushes each = 100K pushes/sec of capacity. 100M / 100K/s = 1000s ≈ 17 min to drain. Auto-scaler adds more workers if lag > 5M.

steps.title: APNs / FCM absorb the sustained 100K/sec
steps.action: Each worker fans across many HTTP/2 streams; APNs allows 1000 concurrent streams per connection. With 200 workers × 5 connections × 1000 streams = 1M stream-slots; 100K in-flight is comfortable.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# throughput math
streams_available = 200 workers * 5 conns * 1000 streams = 1_000_000
in_flight = 100_000 (p50 latency 80ms → 100K * 0.08 = 8K concurrent)

steps.title: Log ingests 100M rows over ~17 min
steps.action: Cassandra writes are partitioned by notification_id so load is uniformly spread. 100M / 1000s = 100K writes/sec — well within a 20-node cluster's capacity.

steps.title: Real-time campaign dashboard
steps.action: Marketing watches delivery progress live: pushes_sent, failure_rate, open_rate (once apps report clicks back). If failure_rate spikes >5% the campaign auto-pauses.
steps.codeOrCommand:
SELECT count_if(status='sent') AS sent, count_if(status='failed') AS failed, sent / estimated_recipients AS progress
FROM notif_attempts
WHERE broadcast_id = '01HWS...'
GROUP BY tumble(created_at, interval '1 minute')

operations.title: 3rd-party gateway timeout — retry with backoff
operations.name: 3rd-party gateway timeout — retry with backoff
operations.description: APNs is brown-out; worker times out; record is re-scheduled onto notif.retry with exponential backoff; second attempt succeeds.

steps.title: Worker picks up a push record
steps.action: A normal notif.push record for user 4782 is picked up by a push worker during an APNs regional brownout.

steps.title: Worker calls APNs with 5s timeout
steps.action: Worker issues the POST on its APNs HTTP/2 stream. The call hangs — no:status after 5000ms. Timeout fires.
steps.codeOrCommand:
try: resp = apns.post(device_token, body, timeout_ms=5000)
except TimeoutError: metrics.counter('apns_timeout_total').inc schedule_retry(rec, delay=backoff(attempt_no=1))

steps.title: APNs does not respond in time
steps.action: The stream stays open but:status never arrives. The TCP keepalive is fine — this is not a connection drop — APNs is just slow under regional load. Circuit breaker counts this timeout toward its threshold.
steps.decision: gateway unresponsive — escalate to retry queue

steps.title: Record attempt 1 as 'failed'
steps.action: Log the failure so operators can trace it. attempt_no=1, status='failed', error_code='apns_timeout'.
steps.codeOrCommand:
INSERT INTO notif_attempts (notification_id, attempt_no, user_id, channel, status, provider, error_code, created_at)
VALUES ('01HWX...', 1, 4782, 'push', 'failed', 'apns', 'timeout', now);

steps.title: Worker publishes to notif.retry with delay
steps.action: Exponential backoff schedule: attempt 1 → delay 1m; 2 → 5m; 3 → 30m; 4 → 2h; 5 → 12h. Worker sets attempt_no=2 and writes to notif.retry with scheduled_at = now+60s. A retry consumer later moves it back to notif.push when due.
steps.codeOrCommand:
delay = backoff_schedule[rec.attempt_no] # 60s
rec.attempt_no += 1
rec.scheduled_at = now + delay
kafka.produce('notif.retry', key=rec.nid, value=rec)

steps.title: notif.retry stores the record
steps.action: A separate retry consumer continuously scans notif.retry and republishes records to their target topic (notif.push here) once scheduled_at <= now. This pattern avoids Kafka's lack of native per-message delay.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# retry-scheduler loop
for rec in retry_consumer.poll: if rec.scheduled_at <= now: kafka.produce(f'notif.{rec.channel}', key=rec.user_id, value=rec) retry_consumer.commit(rec.offset) else: retry_consumer.seek_back sleep(1)

steps.title: 60s later — worker retries and succeeds
steps.action: After the backoff, the retry scheduler moves the record back to notif.push. A worker picks it up; APNs brownout has ended; POST returns:status 200 in 75ms.
steps.codeOrCommand:
resp = apns.post(device_token, body, timeout_ms=5000)
#:status 200, apns-id 7C3F...

steps.title: Record attempt 2 as 'sent'
steps.action: attempt_no=2, status='sent'. The full history is now queryable: attempt 1 failed (timeout), attempt 2 succeeded. Total delivery latency ~62s vs the <1s SLO — a degraded outcome but not a lost notification.
steps.codeOrCommand:
INSERT INTO notif_attempts (notification_id, attempt_no, user_id, channel, status, provider, provider_msg_id, created_at)
VALUES ('01HWX...', 2, 4782, 'push', 'sent', 'apns', '7C3F...', now);

steps.title: Brownout reflected in dashboards
steps.action: The spike in apns_timeout_total and the delayed-delivery p99 feed the reliability dashboard and SLO burn-rate alert. On-call is paged if the brownout persists > 10min.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# Alert rule
- alert: APNsBrownout expr: rate(apns_timeout_total[5m]) > 100 for: 2m labels: { severity: page }

tradeoffs.chosen: Async queue between API and workers
tradeoffs.rationale: Decouples bursty producers from rate-limited vendors; lets the API return 202 in single-digit milliseconds. Cost: the API cannot tell the caller that APNs itself succeeded — only that the request was accepted.

tradeoffs.chosen: Outbox table polled on a schedule, not in-memory timers
tradeoffs.rationale: Worker crashes lose in-memory state; an outbox row survives restarts and is the source of truth for 'what still needs to be retried'. Cost: a DB poller adds a small steady load even when there is nothing to retry.

tradeoffs.chosen: Idempotency key in Redis with 24 h TTL, checked at the API
tradeoffs.rationale: Catches producer-side retries before they hit the queue or the vendor. Cost: Redis is now on the hot path — a Redis outage fails open (best) or fails closed (safer but rejects valid traffic); the design fails open with a short local cache as backup.

tradeoffs.chosen: Separate Kafka topic and worker fleet per channel
tradeoffs.rationale: A Twilio outage cannot starve push or email workers; per-channel tuning (partitions, consumer concurrency) matches the vendor's throughput profile. Cost: more moving parts, more dashboards.

tradeoffs.chosen: Dedicated fan-out service that drips into the normal queues
tradeoffs.rationale: Keeps transactional latency stable during marketing blasts by rate-limiting the burst at the source rather than at the worker. Cost: broadcast campaigns take minutes to fully dispatch, which is acceptable for marketing.

Support scheduled notifications ('send at 9am local time') with timezone-aware dispatch
Add rich notifications with localized templates and A/B test variants
